prime.problem: A dense model has to read every weight for every token, so bigger means proportionally slower. Mixture of experts breaks that link: a huge model can write like a small one. But it still has to fit in memory.
prime.fits: Fourth mechanism card, another way to shrink the bytes side of the bandwidth division. Quantization reads fewer bits per weight; MoE reads fewer weights per token.
expect: memory to hold vs bytes read per token
routing overhead when serving many users
prime.goal: Predict an MoE model's speed ceiling and memory need from its total and active parameters, and decide when it's the right pick.

attend: What does the router decide for each token, and why does that shrink the bytes read?
Why does Qwen3-30B-A3B have the same memory need as a dense 30.5B model but a ~9× higher speed ceiling?
Why can't gpt-oss-120b run on a 24 GB Mac even though it reads only ~2.9 GB per token?
Why is MoE harder to serve efficiently to many users at once?

must: A router picks a few experts per token → only the active slice of weights is read → bytes per token follow active params → speed ceiling ≈ bandwidth ÷ active bytes (≈ 54 t/s for 30B-A3B on the M3)
Any token may need any expert → every expert must stay in memory → memory follows total params → an MoE can be fast yet not fit (gpt-oss-120b: ~66 GB to load)
Writing speed follows active size, knowledge follows total size → big hosted models can still be fast → MoE is the main reason huge models aren't proportionally slow
elevated: Different tokens in a batch want different experts → less weight reuse per read across users → serving many users at once is harder than for a dense model
reference: exact active/total counts (gpt-oss-120b 5.1B of 117B, DeepSeek-V3 37B of 671B)

compress.prompt: From memory, write the two numbers that describe an MoE model and which cost each one controls. Compute the M3 speed ceiling and memory need for a 30B-A3B at 4.5 bits, and write one sentence on when you would choose a dense model instead.
checklist: total params → memory needed to hold it
active params → bytes read per token → speed
30B-A3B: 1.9 GB per token → ≈ 54 t/s ceiling on 100 GB/s; 17.2 GB to hold
choose dense when memory is the limit: at equal memory a dense model is often a bit smarter

retrieve.q: Explain why an MoE model "writes like a small model while knowing like a big one".
answer: per token only the chosen experts' weights are read, so decode cost follows the active params
all experts together store the knowledge, so capability follows total params

retrieve.q: Walk through the arithmetic that gives a dense 30.5B model about 5.8 t/s and the 30B-A3B about 54 t/s on the M3.
Your Mac has 24 GB. Choose between a dense 14B at Q4 and a 30B-A3B at Q4, and name the one thing that could rule out your choice.
answer: 30B-A3B: ~17.2 GB to hold, fits; faster (reads ~1.9 GB vs ~7.9 GB per token)
rule-out: memory headroom for the KV cache, the OS and other apps

compare.q: Quantizing a big dense model 4× vs using an MoE of the same total size: which reads fewer bytes per token, and which needs less memory to load?
answer: MoE reads 9–23× fewer bytes per token
quantizing a dense model cuts both memory and bytes ~4×, but still reads the whole model
quantization wins on memory; MoE wins on speed

compare.q: The hosts card estimates gpt-oss-120b at ~2.7 GB per token and a ~1,240 t/s H100 ceiling. Which MoE fact from this card makes that ceiling possible, and why do real hosts still land far below it?
answer: only 5.1B of 117B params are active, so bytes per token are small
hosts share each chip across many users and add overhead
and MoE batches are harder to serve because tokens want different experts

predict.q: A new MoE has 200B total params and 10B active, at 4.5 bits. Predict its M3 speed ceiling and whether it runs on a 24 GB Mac. Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Active bytes ≈ 10B × 4.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 5.6 GB → ceiling ≈ 100 ÷ 5.6 ≈ 18 t/s. But it needs ≈ 200B × 4.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 112 GB to hold, so it doesn't fit on 24 GB at all. The speed number is irrelevant until the memory number fits.

apply.task: Make a two-column table for three MoE models you could run or rent (use the card's four or look up others): memory to hold (total × bits ÷ 8) and bytes per token (active × bits ÷ 8). Mark which fit in your machine's memory with 4 GB left over, and for those compute the speed ceiling from your bandwidth.
apply.done: Every row has both numbers, the fit/doesn't-fit call is right, and you've named the fastest model that fits.
apply.hint: At 4.5 bits: Qwen3-30B-A3B 17.2 GB / 1.9 GB; gpt-oss-20b ≈ 11.8 GB / 2.0 GB (21B and 3.6B).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the speed ceiling or the fit?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why all experts must stay in memory?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: active params → speed, or total params → quality?
Would an MoE change what you run locally? Which one?
What do you expect speculative decoding to change that neither quantization nor MoE can?
